INTER-FAITH DIALOGUE

OPENING STORY: "THE WORLD FAIR OF RELIGIONS" BY ANTHONY DE MELLO
- The writer and a friend go to "The World Fair of Religions". It is not a trade fair, but the competition is fierce and the propaganda loud.
- Jewish stall: God is All-Compassionate and the Jews are his Chosen People - no other people as chosen as they.
- Muslim stall: God is All-Merciful and Mohammed is his only Prophet. Salvation comes from listening to God's Prophet.
- Christian stall: God is love and there is no salvation outside the Church. Join the Church or risk damnation forever.
- Leaving, the friend says God must be "bigoted, fanatical and cruel".
- At home, the writer asks God how he puts up with this, as they have been giving him a bad name for centuries.
- God replies: "It wasn't I who organised the Fair. In fact, I'd be too ashamed to visit it."
- Message: when religions compete and each claims to be the only true way, they give God a bad name. This exclusive, competitive attitude is the opposite of dialogue.
- Discussion question: Would God be ashamed to visit your country, parish or school?

KEY TERMS (ONE-LINE DEFINITIONS)
- Inter-faith dialogue: dialogue between DIFFERENT faiths, e.g. Christianity and Islam.
- Intra-faith dialogue (ecumenical dialogue): dialogue between different branches of ONE faith, e.g. Catholicism and Anglicanism.
- Ecumenism: the movement for dialogue and unity between Christian churches (mentioned in chapter 1 as a trend in contemporary Ireland).
- World Council of Churches (WCC): a body formed in 1948 with representatives of many major Christian denominations, working for Christian unity.
- Faith: the personal experience of mystery (of God / the transcendent).
- Beliefs: the cultural expression of that faith experience.
- Religious pluralism: many religions existing side by side in one society.
- Multi-faith / multi-ethnic society: a society where people of many creeds (and none) and cultures live together.
- Signals of transcendence: experiences such as deep joy, courage, suffering or death that point beyond ourselves.

BACKGROUND: WHY DIALOGUE MATTERS TODAY
- India and China have been multi-faith societies for many centuries.
- Only in the twentieth century did emigration from Asia, Africa and the Caribbean bring many migrants to Europe, each with their own beliefs and cultures.
- All right-minded people would accept that the only way to live together is through MUTUAL RESPECT, CO-OPERATION and RECONCILIATION.
- Most Western churches accept that there are universal truths in all historic religions.
- The twentieth century saw increased cultural diversity and religious pluralism, with people of all creeds and none living together in multi-ethnic societies.

POPE JOHN PAUL II
- Made significant progress in reaching out to other Christian churches and world religions.
- 1985: called Catholics and Muslims "brothers and sisters in the faith of Abraham".
- 1986: in the Rome synagogue, called Jews "our beloved elder brothers".

VATICAN II - NOSTRA AETATE (PARAGRAPH 2)
- "The Catholic Church rejects nothing in those religions which is true and holy."
- With sincere respect she considers their ways of acting and living, commandments and teachings, which, though different in many ways from her own, "often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all human beings."
- In plain words: the Catholic Church respects what is good and true in other religions and sees in them a ray of God's truth.

THE WORLD COUNCIL OF CHURCHES (WCC)
- Dialogue with people of other religions is an aspiration (hope) of the WCC.
- WCC quote: it commends "the way of dialogue as one in which Jesus Christ can be confessed in the world today" and assures dialogue partners "that we come not as manipulators but as genuine fellow-pilgrims, to speak with them of what we believe God to have done in Jesus Christ."
- In plain words: Christians can share their faith in Christ through dialogue, but honestly, as fellow travellers, not trying to trick or manipulate others.
- Such attempts to heal historic wounds and promote harmony are "the way of inter-faith dialogue".
- Formed in 1948 with representatives from many major Christian denominations.
- It hoped to go beyond institutional or doctrinal (teaching) differences between Christians and build unity like that of the early Christian Church.
- A change in emphasis: the WCC now looks for SPIRITUAL unity rather than organisational or doctrinal unity.

THE ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH AND THE WCC
- The Roman Catholic Church has stayed distant from the WCC.
- It sees itself as living the fullest authentic revelation of Christ's message.
- Catholics argue that Christ did not found a number of churches but ONE Church.
- However, the Catholic Church is committed to ecumenism. It holds that we must all accept responsibility for disunity, which clearly was not in Christ's plan.

S.A. NIGOSIAN: FIVE WAYS CHRISTIAN CHURCHES HAVE RESPONDED TO OTHER RELIGIONS
- 1. EXCLUSIVE perspective: one, and only one, religion is ideal and true; all others are dismissed as false.
- 2. TELEOLOGICAL perspective: one (superior) religion is the completion of all the other (inferior) ones.
- 3. RELATIVE perspective: all religions are different paths to the same goal.
- 4. SINGLE WORLD RELIGION perspective: one global faith will displace or absorb (subsume) all the rest.
- 5. DIALOGIC perspective: promotes communication between faiths to "find a common ground to serve humanity in co-operation with one another".
- Memory tip: E-T-R-S-D (Exclusive, Teleological, Relative, Single world religion, Dialogic).

WHAT REAL DIALOGUE INVOLVES
- Today's world has many and varied types of religious belief and expression - a "complex and rich tapestry" for respectful communication and dialogue.
- We cannot live with an INDIFFERENT attitude of tolerance, nor with ANGRY confrontation.
- Dialogue is a challenging encounter that helps build peace and justice among people of all creeds and cultures.
- Dialogue challenges existing opinions and prejudices.

FAITH AND BELIEFS
- Authentic dialogue distinguishes between faith and beliefs.
- Faith = the personal experience of mystery.
- Beliefs = the cultural expression of this faith experience.
- There is an unbreakable bond between faith and beliefs.
- But the "signals of transcendence" (experiences such as deep joy, courage, suffering or death) can never be fully and completely expressed in beliefs. To claim they could would limit faith experience.
- So people of different beliefs may share a deeper faith experience; this makes dialogue possible.

FORMS OF DIALOGUE IN PRACTICE
- International conferences: many theologians and scholars (including Roman Catholics) meet for inter-denominational and inter-faith dialogue.
- They explore concepts such as the existence of suffering and evil, and the mystery of life, in a non-threatening, non-competitive environment.
- Inter-faith worship: another initiative to foster harmony and acceptance.
- Inter-faith prayer rooms in airports and shopping centres give people a place for "time-out" - a spiritual experience rather than an institutionalised ritual.

A PARADIGM SHIFT IN SPIRITUALITY
- The worldwide spiritual search has led, in this century, to a paradigm shift (a major change in thinking).
- Many members of all faiths (and none) now direct their own spiritual journey within communities that offer a framework that answers their needs.
- PROFESSOR JAMES W. FOWLER: a significant number of believers have taken personal responsibility for how they take on their traditions and how they integrate religious teachings into their lives. They base their faith on their own reflective judgements and experiences.
- Fowler says the recent use of the word "spiritual" to describe one's personal faith reflects a commitment to a "postconventional" claiming of authority for one's own religious and ethical orientation and practices (people deciding for themselves rather than simply following convention).

THE JOURNEY OF FAITH
- People come to know God through COMMUNITY, PRAYER, WORSHIP and SCRIPTURE.
- The journey may be joyful and confident, or sad and confused, or even self-righteous or indifferent.
- We hope every opportunity to dialogue with other denominations and faiths will inform, challenge and mature us.

PAUL F. KNITTER
- The task demanded of Christianity and all religions is that they "speak and listen to each other", "grow with and from each other", and "combine efforts for the welfare, the salvation, of all humanity".
- If this is done, the central hopes of all religions will come closer: "Allah will be known and praised; Lord Krishna will act in the world; enlightenment will be furthered and deepened; God's kingdom will be understood and promoted."
- Message: dialogue helps every religion achieve its own deepest goals (Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Christianity).

THREE WAYS NATIONS LET PEOPLE OF FAITH LIVE TOGETHER (FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS)
- 1. A SECULAR STATE: the Government is kept apart from any association with religion.
- 2. An ESTABLISHED CHURCH, with full recognition of minority faiths.
- 3. A RELIGIOUS STATE, demanding acceptance of one faith.

FAITHS THAT CROSS RELIGIOUS BOUNDARIES (FROM THE ASSIGNMENTS)
- Baha'is: a vision of a simple global religion promoting unity and peace.
- Sikhs: believe in the unity and oneness of all people and accept the legitimacy of all faiths.
- These contrast with the teaching of exclusivity held by some other world faiths.

QUALITIES NEEDED IN A MULTI-FAITH SOCIETY (FROM THE CHAPTER'S THEMES)
- Mutual respect, co-operation, reconciliation, openness to truth in other religions, willingness to listen and be challenged, honesty (not manipulation).

CHAPTER KEY TERMS LIST
- Inter-faith dialogue, Intra-faith dialogue, Ecumenism, World Council of Churches, Faith and beliefs.

rows.prompt: Explain the difference between inter-faith dialogue and intra-faith dialogue, giving an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Inter-faith dialogue is dialogue between different faiths, for example between Christianity and Islam. Intra-faith (or ecumenical) dialogue is dialogue between different branches of one faith, for example between Catholicism and Anglicanism.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words the message of Anthony de Mello's story 'The World Fair of Religions'.
rows.model_answer: At the fair each religion claimed to be the only true way - the Jews as the only chosen people, the Muslims with the only Prophet, and the Christians saying there is no salvation outside the Church. This rivalry made God look 'bigoted, fanatical and cruel'. God says he would be too ashamed to visit, showing that competition and exclusive claims give God a bad name.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words the message of Nostra aetate, paragraph 2.
rows.model_answer: The Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. It respects their ways of living, commandments and teachings, even where they differ from its own, because they often reflect a ray of the Truth that enlightens all people.

rows.prompt: Give two examples of Pope John Paul II reaching out to other religions.
rows.model_answer: In 1985 he referred to Catholics and Muslims as 'brothers and sisters in the faith of Abraham'. In 1986, in the Rome synagogue, he spoke of Jews as 'our beloved elder brothers'.

rows.prompt: What is the World Council of Churches and what does it aim to do?
rows.model_answer: The WCC was formed in 1948 with representatives of many major Christian denominations. It hoped to go beyond institutional and doctrinal differences and build unity like that of the early Church. Its emphasis has changed to seeking spiritual unity rather than organisational or doctrinal unity.

rows.prompt: Name three of S.A. Nigosian's perspectives and explain each in one sentence.
rows.model_answer: Exclusive: only one religion is true and all others are false. Relative: all religions are different paths to the same goal. Dialogic: faiths communicate to find common ground to serve humanity together. (Others: teleological - one superior religion completes the others; single world religion - one global faith replaces or absorbs the rest.)

rows.prompt: Explain the distinction between faith and beliefs and why it matters for dialogue.
rows.model_answer: Faith is the personal experience of mystery, while beliefs are the cultural expression of that experience. The two are bound together, but experiences such as deep joy, courage, suffering or death can never be fully expressed in beliefs. Authentic dialogue recognises this, so people of different beliefs can respect a shared depth of faith.

rows.prompt: Describe the three ways nations allow people of faith to live together.
rows.model_answer: A secular state keeps the Government apart from any association with religion. An established church is the official church but gives full recognition to minority faiths. A religious state demands the acceptance of one faith.

rows.prompt: Outline the five ways in which, according to S.A. Nigosian, Christian churches have responded to other religions. Which response best supports inter-faith dialogue? Explain.
rows.model_answer: S.A. Nigosian says Christian churches have responded to religious pluralism in five ways. The exclusive perspective accepts one, and only one, religion as ideal and true and dismisses all others as false. The teleological perspective sees one superior religion as the completion of all the other, inferior, ones. The relative perspective sees all religions as different paths to the same goal. The single world religion perspective expects one global faith to displace or absorb all the rest. The dialogic perspective promotes communication between faiths to 'find a common ground to serve humanity in co-operation with one another'. The dialogic perspective best supports inter-faith dialogue. The exclusive view creates the kind of competition shown in Anthony de Mello's 'World Fair of Religions', where rival claims made God seem 'bigoted, fanatical and cruel'. The dialogic view, by contrast, avoids both indifferent tolerance and angry confrontation. It treats dialogue as a challenging encounter that questions prejudices and builds peace and justice. This matches the WCC's wish to meet others 'not as manipulators but as genuine fellow-pilgrims', and Paul F. Knitter's call for religions to speak and listen to each other and combine efforts for the welfare of all humanity.
rows.marking_scheme: Outline five perspectives: 5 x 2 marks = 10 (name 1 + explain 1). Evaluation: 10 marks - very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. Should choose a perspective (normally dialogic) and justify it with reference to e.g. de Mello, WCC 'fellow-pilgrims', Knitter, rejecting indifference and confrontation, challenging prejudice, building peace and justice.

rows.prompt: Describe the work of the World Council of Churches and the attitude of the Roman Catholic Church towards ecumenism.
rows.model_answer: The World Council of Churches (WCC) was formed in 1948 with representatives from many major Christian denominations. It hoped to go beyond the institutional and doctrinal differences between Christians and build the kind of unity seen in the early Christian Church. It also sees dialogue with people of other religions as important. It commends dialogue as a way in which Jesus Christ can be confessed today, while assuring partners that Christians 'come not as manipulators but as genuine fellow-pilgrims'. Over time its emphasis has changed: it now looks for spiritual unity rather than organisational or doctrinal unity. The Roman Catholic Church has remained distant from the WCC, because it considers itself to be living the fullest authentic revelation of Christ's message. Catholics argue that Christ did not found a number of churches but one Church. However, the Catholic Church is committed to ecumenism and holds that all must accept responsibility for disunity, which was clearly not in Christ's plan. Its openness is seen in Vatican II's Nostra aetate, which 'rejects nothing ... which is true and holy' in other religions, and in Pope John Paul II's outreach to Muslims in 1985 and Jews in 1986.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: WCC 1948; many denominations; going beyond doctrinal/institutional differences; early Church unity; 'fellow-pilgrims' quote; shift to spiritual unity; Catholic distance - fullest revelation, one Church; commitment to ecumenism; shared responsibility for disunity; Nostra aetate; John Paul II examples. Both parts needed for top band.

rows.prompt: 'Dialogue challenges existing opinions and prejudices.' Discuss what authentic inter-faith dialogue involves.
rows.model_answer: In today's world there are many varied types of religious belief, giving a 'complex and rich tapestry' for respectful dialogue. Authentic dialogue rejects two extremes: an indifferent attitude of tolerance, where people simply ignore each other, and angry confrontation. Instead it is a challenging encounter that helps build peace and justice among people of all creeds and cultures, and it questions existing opinions and prejudices. Authentic dialogue distinguishes between faith, the personal experience of mystery, and beliefs, the cultural expression of that experience. Faith and beliefs are bound together, but 'signals of transcendence' such as deep joy, courage, suffering or death can never be fully captured in beliefs. Realising this helps people see that others may share a deep faith experience even if their beliefs differ. In practice, theologians and scholars meet at international conferences to explore suffering, evil and the mystery of life in a non-threatening, non-competitive way, and inter-faith prayer rooms in airports and shopping centres offer shared spiritual space. Dialogue also needs honesty: the WCC comes 'not as manipulators but as genuine fellow-pilgrims'. As Paul F. Knitter says, religions must speak and listen to each other and grow with and from each other.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: rich tapestry; not indifferent tolerance or angry confrontation; challenging encounter building peace and justice; challenges prejudice; faith vs beliefs; signals of transcendence; international conferences; inter-faith worship/prayer rooms; honesty ('fellow-pilgrims'); Knitter; mutual respect, co-operation, reconciliation. Must discuss, not just list.

rows.prompt: Outline two examples of the Catholic Church's openness to other world religions.
rows.model_answer: First, the Second Vatican Council, in Nostra aetate (paragraph 2), taught that 'the Catholic Church rejects nothing in those religions which is true and holy'. It respects their ways of acting and living, their commandments and teachings, which, although they differ in many respects from Catholic teaching, 'often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all human beings'. This shows respect for what is good in other faiths. Second, Pope John Paul II made significant progress in reaching out to other churches and religions. In 1985 he referred to Catholics and Muslims as 'brothers and sisters in the faith of Abraham', and in 1986, in the Rome synagogue, he spoke of Jews as 'our beloved elder brothers'. These words recognised shared roots and helped heal historic wounds between the faiths.
rows.marking_scheme: Two examples x 5 marks (identify 2 + explain 3). Examples: Nostra aetate - rejects nothing true and holy, ray of Truth; John Paul II 1985 Muslims 'brothers and sisters in the faith of Abraham'; John Paul II 1986 Rome synagogue 'beloved elder brothers'; Catholic theologians at inter-faith conferences.
